vignette:
The Weight of the Operating Room

Boon-Nam is a 77-year-old Thai-born surgeon who has spent the better part of five decades with his hands inside the human body, repairing what has broken. He is precise, methodical, and quietly proud of a career that has saved countless lives. His wife of fifty-one years describes him as a man who has always known what to do in a crisis. That certainty, she says, is gone now.

Eighteen months ago, Boon-Nam was assisting a younger colleague - a surgeon he had mentored for years - during a complex hepatic resection. What began as a routine procedure deteriorated rapidly. A catastrophic hemorrhage, a series of decisions made under desperate pressure, and then nothing more could be done. His colleague collapsed at the scrub sink shortly after the patient was pronounced dead. Boon-Nam watched the man he had trained fall to the floor of the operating theater, seizing violently, the product of what would later be identified as a massive stroke. He knelt beside him on the cold tile, holding his colleague's head in his gloved hands, calling his name, until the emergency team arrived. His colleague survived, but with profound neurological damage. He will not operate again. He does not always recognize Boon-Nam when he visits.

In the weeks that followed, Boon-Nam returned to the operating theater because he did not know what else to do. He is semi-retired but still performs elective procedures several days a week. He found, to his horror, that he could not trust his own hands. Not because they trembled - they did not - but because his mind would leave the room. He would be standing at the table, retractor in hand, and suddenly he would be back on that floor, the fluorescent lights above him, the sound of his colleague's breathing changing into something wrong and animal. He began requesting longer instrument counts, double-checking closures he had performed ten thousand times, arriving an hour early to review cases he could recite from memory. The scrub nurses noticed. He pretended not to notice that they noticed.

At home, Boon-Nam sleeps in three-hour intervals. He wakes at two or three in the morning with his heart already racing, the images from that day arriving before he is fully conscious. He does not wake his wife. He goes to his study and reads surgical journals until the sky lightens, absorbing information he no longer fully retains. He has stopped attending the monthly dinner with the colleagues he has known for thirty years. The noise of a crowded restaurant, the clink of glasses, the sudden burst of laughter - these things make him feel as though he is standing at the edge of something he cannot name.

He is irritable in ways that are new to him. His wife asks a simple question and he answers with a sharpness that surprises them both. He apologizes. He does not explain. He has not told her the full shape of what he carries, because he believes, with the conviction of his generation and his training, that a man who has witnessed suffering his entire professional life should be able to absorb this too. He is a surgeon. He has held dying people in his hands. This is simply one more.

And yet he finds himself, on quiet afternoons in his study, replaying the sequence of events with the obsessive precision of a clinician searching for an error - not in the surgery, but in himself. Could he have seen it coming? Should he have insisted his colleague rest? The questions do not resolve. They only accumulate.

He came to therapy at his wife's gentle, persistent urging. He sat down in the chair across from the therapist, folded his hands in his lap, and said, in his careful, formal English: I am not sure I am the kind of person this is meant for. Then he began to talk, and he did not stop for the full hour.
